Creating The Right Mood For a Performance; Series 3 Some years ago, my wife and I were scheduled to minister with our church choir on a Sunday morning. Like every other performance, we came prepared, expecting to give our best in the worship and praise session. But that morning, just before the service, we received news that completely changed our mood: our home had been flooded after a heavy downpour. Immediately, our thoughts went home. What had happened to our properties? How bad was the damage? What would we find when we eventually returned home? There were so many unanswered questions running through our minds. Our emotions were shattered. Our excitement disappeared. Honestly, it was difficult to think about standing before the congregation and singing as though everything was fine. But then, something happened. We remembered that we were not simply going on stage to sing songs. We had a responsibility to help create the right atmosphere for worship and praise. The congregation was expecting us to lead them into an atmosphere of celebration, thanksgiving and worship. We couldn’t allow our personal situation to completely determine the atmosphere we were expected to create. So, we made a conscious decision. We switched into the right mood for the performance. It wasn’t because the problem had disappeared. It hadn’t. Our house was still flooded. Our properties were still at risk. The questions were still unanswered. But we understood something important: professionalism and discipline sometimes require you to perform beyond your immediate emotions. Years of training and serving in music had taught us that a performer cannot always wait until they “feel like it” before giving their best. There will be days when you are tired, worried, disappointed, emotionally drained or dealing with personal challenges. Yet, when the responsibility comes, you must learn how to manage those emotions and focus on the assignment. That morning, we stepped forward and did what we had been trained to do. We worshipped. We praised. We encouraged the congregation. And, for those moments, we deliberately put aside what was happening at home and gave ourselves to the performance. Looking back, that experience taught me one of the most important lessons about performing: The right mood is not always the mood you naturally wake up with. Sometimes, it is the mood you intentionally create. Your Emotions Are Real, But They Don’t Always Have to Lead This doesn’t mean performers should pretend that their problems don’t exist. We are human. Things happen. You can receive unpleasant news, have a difficult morning, experience disappointment or walk into a performance carrying a heavy heart. But you must learn to ask yourself: “What does this performance require from me?” A worship session may require reverence and sensitivity. A praise session may require energy and joy. A concert may require excitement and engagement. A solemn presentation may require restraint and emotional depth. Understanding what the moment requires helps you prepare your mind for the performance. Training Builds This Discipline This is one reason I strongly believe in proper training for singers and musicians. Training is not only about learning notes, chords, rhythms, breathing techniques or stage movement. Training also develops discipline, emotional control, adaptability and responsibility. A trained performer understands that not every performance will happen under perfect circumstances. Sometimes the sound system will disappoint you. Sometimes another musician will make a mistake. Sometimes you will be physically tired. Sometimes you will have personal issues on your mind. The ability to remain focused and still deliver appropriately is part of musicianship. The Audience Doesn’t Always Know What You’re Carrying One of the things I have learned over the years is that the audience may never know what the performer is going through internally. They may see your smile. They may hear your voice. They may see your confidence. But they may not know that, just hours earlier, you received devastating news. That is why performers must develop the ability to separate personal emotions from performance responsibility when necessary. Of course, there are situations where the emotional burden is too great, and stepping back is the right decision. But when you are able to perform, discipline allows you to focus on the moment and serve the audience or congregation effectively. That Sunday morning remains a reminder to me that great performances are not always produced under perfect circumstances. Sometimes, they come from moments when you have every reason to lose focus, yet you choose to remain committed to the assignment. Get your mind ready. Understand the mood required. Manage your emotions. Trust your preparation. Creating The Right Mood For a Performance; Series 2 What Experience Has Taught Me Over the years of performing, directing choirs, training singers, and working with musicians, I have learned something that may not be found in a music theory book: your emotional state can influence your performance just as much as your musical preparation. I remember occasions when I arrived at a performance venue technically prepared. I knew my songs, understood the arrangement, rehearsed with the team, and was confident that everything would go well. Yet, somehow, the performance did not feel as good as I expected. On other occasions, I have walked onto a stage after a difficult or stressful day, but something changed the moment the music began. I deliberately shifted my attention from whatever was happening around me to the purpose of the performance. My mind became calmer, my focus improved, and I was able to connect with the audience and the music. That experience taught me that being ready to perform is not only about knowing what to sing or play; it is also about being mentally and emotionally ready to perform. Your Mood Can Affect Your Performance A singer who is anxious may struggle with breathing, pitch, confidence, or expression. A musician who is distracted may miss cues or make mistakes. A choir that comes on stage carrying tension from rehearsals may sound technically correct but lack warmth and connection. This does not mean we must always feel happy before performing. That is unrealistic. Rather, we must learn how to manage our emotions and intentionally create the right performance mindset. Before I perform or lead a team, I try to ask myself: What is the purpose of this performance? What atmosphere do we want to create? What does the audience need from us? Those questions help me move my attention away from unnecessary distractions and toward the performance itself. The Right Mood Doesn’t Happen by Accident One thing experience has taught me is that the mood for a performance often begins before you get on stage. How you arrive at the venue matters. How you respond when something goes wrong during rehearsal matters. Even the conversation you have immediately before walking onto the stage can influence the atmosphere. This is why I encourage musicians and singers to avoid unnecessary arguments, negative conversations, panic, and last-minute confusion before performing. Take a moment | Breathe | Listen Pray or reflect, if appropriate. Review your first entry and important cues. Then remind yourself why you are there. Don’t Confuse Energy With Noise Having the right mood does not necessarily mean becoming excessively excited. Sometimes the best performance preparation is quiet. A singer may need a few minutes of silence before going on stage. A choir may need to gather together and mentally settle. A band may need to focus on communication rather than joking around immediately before a performance. The goal is not to manufacture an emotion. The goal is to create the emotional and mental space that allows you to perform at your best. Preparation Gives You Confidence I have also discovered that the right mood becomes much easier to achieve when you have prepared properly. It is difficult to feel calm when you don’t know your music. It is difficult to feel confident when you haven’t rehearsed your transitions. It is difficult to connect with your audience when you are still wondering what comes next. Good preparation reduces unnecessary anxiety. When you know your material, understand your role, trust your team, and have rehearsed possible challenges, you have more freedom to focus on expression and connection. The Performance Begins Before the First Note Today, I see performance preparation differently. The performance does not begin when the microphone is switched on or when the conductor raises his hands. It begins in your mind before you step onto the stage. Learn to leave unnecessary distractions behind. Learn to manage nervousness. Learn to encourage your team. Learn to understand the atmosphere you are trying to create. Because sometimes, the difference between an ordinary performance and a memorable one is not another rehearsal.
